title: Cerebellar Residual Control for Robot Fault Recovery
one_liner: A robot can fix post-training faults without retraining by adding a small, fast cerebellar-inspired correction layer that learns from real errors at deployment time.
lead: When a robot leaves the lab and a motor breaks or the ground shifts, it cannot stop to retrain. Instead, this paper attaches a small corrective system that works like the brain's cerebellum: it reads a fixed set of details about what the robot senses, runs them through a frozen lookup table, and learns tiny local fixes that steer the robot back on course. The main policy stays untouched; the correction layer captures only the gap between what the robot tried and what actually happened.

problem.h2: Robots break. Retraining is not an option.
paras: A robot policy is trained in the lab under ideal conditions: clean motors, predictable ground, perfect sensors. Once deployed to a warehouse or hospital, the robot might encounter faults: a motor becomes stiff, the surface is icy, a sensor drifts. The usual fix is to stop, collect new data on the fault, and retrain the policy from scratch. But stopping a deployed robot is expensive, often unsafe, and retraining requires exploration that may damage the system further.

A beginner might try to teach the robot to handle all possible faults during training by deliberately breaking it in many ways, then learning a policy that survives these faults. This fails because no training can cover every real fault the robot will see. Instead, the robot arrives at the factory floor encountering a fault no one predicted, and its learned policy is useless.

callout.html: The policy works perfectly in training but fails at deployment when the world changes.

steps.text: Take the robot's current state (position, speed, joint angles) and run it through a fixed, random lookup table to create hundreds of new features.
Split those features into small groups, each assigned to its own parallel mini-corrector, so faults in different parts of the body get fixed separately.
Each micro-corrector sums its features with learned weights and outputs a small adjustment to the robot's commands.
After the robot moves, compare what happened to what should happen and measure the gap (the actual outcome minus predicted).
Tag which features led to that error with fast and slow time-scales, so learning is both immediate and stable.

object.h2: The object: the corrective residual layer
paras: The paper modifies one thing: it adds a second control layer that works in parallel with the frozen main policy. This residual layer is small, operates only at deployment, and learns from real errors without touching the original policy. The base policy remains completely unchanged; the residual layer is pure addition.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: the fault signal, measured by error
hidden.name: Temporal error
paras: The paper measures one key hidden quantity: the prediction error, the gap between what the robot intended and what actually happened. At each moment, the robot predicts the outcome of its chosen action. The real world delivers a different outcome (because of the fault). That gap is the signal.

The residual layer learns by seeing this error: it observes which features were present when the error occurred, marks them (via eligibility traces, a biological learning signal), and gently adjusts those features' weights so similar errors shrink next time. The error is estimated online at deployment without any explicit fault model.

heat.caption: Darker: features and traces that carry fault information. Marked cells are central to the cerebellar principle of localized, parallel correction.

reads.html: The error is simply how wrong the robot was: intended to move forward 10 cm but moved 7 cm. That gap tells the corrector which features mattered and how to adjust them.

The paper computes temporal difference errors (the gap between the value function prediction at time t and the actual observed reward plus the value at t+1) and uses those to weight eligibility traces for biological-style credit assignment.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: cerebellar learning without global retraining
paras: The mechanism has three parts. First, a fixed feature expansion: the robot's raw state (10 numbers) is run through a random lookup table to create 500 new features. This expansion is like shining a light on the state from many angles, so tiny faults become visible differences in the expanded features. The expansion is fixed (never learned), so it adds no new weights to learn and no stability risk.

Second, parallel microzone pathways: instead of one global corrector, the 500 features are split into small groups of 50 each, with 10 separate mini-correctors running in parallel. When a motor in the shoulder sticks, the features tied to that shoulder activate; the shoulder's microzone learns the correction; the hip's microzone is undisturbed. This parallelism is the core cerebellar principle: faults are local, so fixes can be local, avoiding the risk that fixing the shoulder breaks the hip.

Third, eligibility traces with two time scales. When an error occurs, the features that were present get marked. A fast mark decays quickly (say, 50 milliseconds), capturing immediate cause-and-effect. A slow mark decays over seconds, capturing delayed effects. Both marks are updated with small, learned weights. This dual-timescale learning is stable: the fast trace moves aggressively to fix immediate faults, the slow trace anchors long-term behavior. Together they enable the corrector to learn in seconds or minutes at deployment because the fast trace reacts immediately to errors (a motor sticks, the error appears, the trace fires, the weight shifts) without waiting for the long timescale convergence that would take hours. The slow trace then smooths out noise so the fast learning does not oscillate wildly.

stages.s: Raw state: 10 joint angles and speeds
Fixed expansion: random lookup table produces 500 features
Route to 10 parallel micro-correctors, 50 features each
Each computes weighted sum of its features
Update weights via fast and slow eligibility traces
Corrective action added to frozen base policy

math.words: residual action equals the sum over all micro-zones of the sum of (learned weight times that zone's basis function feature), where each weight is updated proportionally to the error times the eligibility trace
math.equation: a_residual(t) = sum_z sum_i w_i^z(t) * phi_i^z(state) ; w_i^z(t+1) = w_i^z(t) + alpha * error(t) * e_i^z(t)
symbols: the small correction added to the base policy action
a microzone index (1 to 10, one per body region)
a feature index within that zone (1 to 50)
the learned weight for feature i in zone z
the fixed basis function value for that feature
the robot's current position, speed, angles
outcome minus prediction, the temporal difference
the eligibility trace, decays over time
the learning rate, how big each update is

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the hip microzone has 5 features. The state activates features with values [0.3, 0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.0].
Learned weights for those features are [0.8, 0.2, 1.2, 0.5, 0.3].
At that moment, the robot tried to move forward 2 cm but moved 1.5 cm (error = 0.5 cm shortfall).
Fast trace values for those features are [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.2, 0.0] (recent activity).
Update: weight 0 becomes 0.8 + 0.1*0.5*1.0 = 0.8 + 0.05 = 0.85 (pulled up because that feature was active during an undershooting error).
Weights for inactive features stay the same. This small, localized adjustment is repeated at every time step during deployment.

math.note: The learning rate alpha is tiny (typically 0.01 or less), so each update is a gentle nudge. Over hours of deployment, these nudges accumulate and the weights converge to corrections that fix the fault.

bars.h2: Performance under faults: naive, pre-trained-for-faults, and learned-during-deployment

charts.title: Frozen base policy (no correction)
charts.note: Without any adaptation, the policy collapses under any fault. It was trained in the nominal world only.

charts.title: Policy trained on deliberate faults (pre-exposure approach)
charts.note: By deliberately breaking the robot during training and learning a policy that survives these faults, performance holds on faults the robot saw before. But new faults are still catastrophic because training cannot cover the infinite space of possible faults.

charts.title: Cerebellar residual (inference-time learning)
rows: Moderate fault (never seen, learns in 1 minute)
charts.note: The residual layer learns corrections on the fly. Even unseen faults are gracefully handled because the cerebellar error signal is universal: any gap between prediction and reality is correctable. Performance improves over deployment time because each error immediately triggers a weight update (via the fast eligibility trace), so every fault the robot encounters teaches the corrector to fix that specific fault, not just the faults it saw during training.

items.b: The lookup table must not change during deployment.
items.html: If the random lookup table that expands the state into features is modified during deployment, or if the features are not truly random and structured, the cerebellar layer can overfit to noise and lose generalization. The paper uses fixed, random features to ensure stability across different fault types.

items.b: The error signal must be accurate.
items.html: If the robot cannot measure what actually happened (e.g., the sensors are broken or too noisy), the error signal is garbage and the cerebellar layer learns the wrong corrections. The paper assumes accurate state feedback, which is reasonable for many robots but fragile if sensors degrade.

If the brain tried to correct a global property (like overall energy efficiency) using local, zone-by-zone adjustments, the zones would fight each other and learning would diverge. The method works only when faults are local and regions can be corrected independently.

When the fault is local, the error signal is clean, and the robot can measure state accurately, the cerebellar approach recovers performance in minutes, stays stable, and does not modify the base policy, preserving the nominal behavior the original training achieved.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train a simple robot policy (a 2-link arm or a walking creature) in MuJoCo under nominal conditions. Freeze the policy. Inject a post-training fault (add stiffness to a motor, scale down an action by 30%, or shift the ground angle by 5 degrees) without retraining. Add the cerebellar residual layer and let it train online for 60 seconds of real deployment. Measure: (1) how much performance recovers, (2) how much the base policy parameters change (they should not), (3) how stable the recovery is over the next fault severity.
demo.closing: The demo must show that a robot broken at deployment can recover 60 to 80 percent of nominal performance in under a minute, without retraining or exploration, and the base policy stays completely frozen throughout.
